title: Hargeisa Youth Join Growing Coding Movement
excerpt: More young people in Hargeisa are learning programming and building apps for local businesses.
content:
Coding clubs and training centres in Hargeisa are seeing record interest from young people.

Students are building websites and simple apps for shops, schools and local organisations, turning new skills into real income.

FIKRADO Security continues to offer free and subsidised seats for students in need.

title: Mobile Money Keeps Somaliland Among the World's Most Cashless Places
excerpt: Paying by phone is now normal in Somaliland markets, raising new needs for digital security.
content:
Mobile money services are used for almost everything in Somaliland, from buying vegetables to paying school fees.

This convenience makes strong security essential: protecting PINs, spotting SIM-swap scams and keeping phones updated.

FIKRADO runs awareness sessions to help users and merchants stay safe.

title: Ethiopia's Tech Hubs Train a New Generation of Engineers
excerpt: Innovation centres in Addis Ababa and beyond are training youth in AI, robotics and drone technology.
content:
Ethiopia is investing in technology talent through innovation hubs and national AI efforts.

Young engineers are working on drones, smart agriculture and AI tools built for local needs.

FIKRADO's Jijiga branch supports this growth with practical AI and cybersecurity training.

title: Ethiopia Expands Digital Government Services
excerpt: More public services are moving online, increasing the need for skilled cybersecurity professionals.
content:
Ethiopia is bringing more government services online, from ID registration to payments.

As systems go digital, protecting citizen data becomes a top priority, creating strong demand for cybersecurity skills across the country.

title: AI Agents Move From Demos to Daily Work
excerpt: Companies are deploying AI agents that plan and complete multi-step tasks, from booking travel to triaging support tickets.
content:
AI agents — systems that can plan, use tools and finish multi-step tasks — are moving out of research demos and into everyday business software.

Teams are using them to triage support tickets, draft reports and automate repetitive back-office work. The biggest lesson so far: agents work best with clear goals, limited permissions and a human reviewing important actions.

For learners in Somalia and the region, understanding how to design and supervise agents is quickly becoming a valuable skill.

title: Open-Weight AI Models Close the Gap
excerpt: Freely available models are now strong enough for many real projects, lowering the cost of building with AI.
content:
Open-weight language models have improved rapidly and now handle many tasks that once needed expensive paid services.

This matters for students and startups: a capable model can run on a single rented GPU, or even a laptop for smaller versions, keeping data private and costs low.

The trade-off is responsibility — teams running their own models must handle safety, updates and evaluation themselves.

title: AI Becomes a Double-Edged Sword in Cybersecurity
excerpt: Attackers use AI to write convincing phishing, while defenders use it to spot threats faster.
content:
Security teams are seeing more AI-written phishing emails that read naturally in many languages, including Somali.

At the same time, defenders use AI to summarise alerts, find suspicious patterns in logs and speed up incident response.

The basics still matter most: multi-factor authentication, updated software and staff who know how to recognise a scam.

title: AI Tutors Expand Learning Across Africa
excerpt: Low-cost AI tutoring tools are helping students practise maths, coding and languages on basic phones.
content:
AI-powered tutoring tools are reaching more students across Africa, often through simple chat apps on low-cost phones.

Teachers report that students practise more when they can ask questions at any time. The challenge is quality in local languages, and making sure tools support teachers rather than replace them.

FIKRADO is exploring Somali-language learning content built with these tools.

title: Multimodal AI Can Now See, Hear and Speak
excerpt: New models understand images, audio and video alongside text in a single conversation.
content:
The latest AI models are multimodal: they can read a photo of a document, listen to speech and reply with a natural voice.

Practical uses include reading handwritten forms, describing images for visually impaired users and real-time translation.

For developers, this means one model can replace several separate tools.

title: Governments Draft New Rules for AI
excerpt: More countries are introducing laws on transparency, safety testing and data use for AI systems.
content:
Governments around the world are writing rules for AI, focusing on transparency, safety testing of powerful models and protection of personal data.

Businesses building with AI should keep records of how models are used and be ready to explain automated decisions.

East African policymakers are also discussing national AI strategies.

title: AI Coding Assistants Change How Software Is Built
excerpt: Developers use AI to write, test and explain code — but reviewing it remains essential.
content:
AI coding assistants now write large parts of everyday code, generate tests and explain unfamiliar projects.

Experienced developers say the skill has shifted from typing code to describing problems clearly and carefully reviewing what the AI produces.

Beginners still need strong fundamentals so they can tell good code from bad.

title: AI Helps Doctors Read Scans Faster
excerpt: Hospitals are testing AI that flags possible problems in X-rays and scans for doctors to review.
content:
AI tools that analyse medical images are being tested in more hospitals, helping doctors prioritise urgent cases.

In areas with few specialists, this could shorten waiting times significantly. Experts stress that the final decision must stay with trained medical staff.

title: The Energy Cost of AI Comes Into Focus
excerpt: Data centres powering AI use huge amounts of electricity, pushing research into more efficient models.
content:
Training and running large AI models consumes a lot of electricity and water for cooling.

This is driving work on smaller, more efficient models and on placing data centres near renewable energy.

Efficient models are also good news for regions with limited infrastructure.

title: Push Grows for Better Somali-Language AI
excerpt: Researchers and communities are collecting Somali text and speech to improve AI support for the language.
content:
Most AI systems still perform worse in Somali than in English because there is less training data.

Community projects are now gathering Somali text, speech recordings and translations to change that.

Better Somali AI would open up education, government services and business tools to millions more people.

title: FIKRADO Security Opens Free Cyber Training Cohort in Hargeisa
excerpt: A three-month, non-profit cohort teaching ethical hacking, Linux and networking fundamentals to students across Somaliland.
content:
FIKRADO Security has opened applications for its next free cyber training cohort in Hargeisa.

The programme runs for twelve weeks and covers network fundamentals, Linux administration, and an introduction to ethical hacking. Sessions are delivered in Somali and English, and every participant finishes with a practical portfolio rather than only theory.

Because FIKRADO is a 50% non-profit, the cohort is free for selected students. Places are limited and allocated through a short application and a practical aptitude exercise.

Interested readers can register interest through the contact page and mention the cohort name in their message.

title: Hands-On AI Workshop Completed in Jijiga
excerpt: Participants built small AI projects end to end — from data collection to a working demo — during a two-day workshop.
content:
Our two-day applied AI workshop in Jijiga wrapped up with every participant shipping a working demo.

Rather than a lecture series, the workshop was structured around building. Attendees collected a small dataset, trained a baseline model, and then presented their results to the room.

The most common piece of feedback was that the constraint that mattered most was not compute — it was knowing how to frame a problem that a model could actually be evaluated against.

We will run a follow-up session focused on evaluation and deployment, with places announced in a future post.
